No evidence supports the contention that Harmony Moller’s use of kratom contributed to her death. The postmortem concentration of mitragynine identified in Ms. Moller’s blood was 158 ng/mL as measured by the Gerona lab (St. Tammany Parish Coroner records); commercial clinical laboratories measured the mitragynine concentration as 150 ng/mL (St. Tammany Parish Coroner records). Mitragynine undergoes postmortem redistribution, a process where the concentration of a substance changes following death. The available scientific literature demonstrates that the postmortem concentration of mitragynine is approximately triple that of pre- mortem measurements (Osawa 2025). To a reasonable degree of medical certainty, therefore, Ms. Moller’s premortem concentration of mitragynine was approximately 50 ng/mL, a value that occurred in human clinical trials involving kratom. Notably, none of the participants in these studies developed cardiac toxicity, much less a life-threatening event. Ms. Moller did not die from her kratom use. 76. In fact, medical examiners initially noted that the cause of death was “chronic liver congestion.” Chronic liver congestion is a medical condition often associated with right heart failure; backup of blood (i.e., “congestion”) into the liver produces fibrotic changes that become apparent even on visual inspection of the liver. Notably, kratom has not been associated with chronic liver congestion, even among patients where right heart failure was putatively associated with distant and undefined kratom ingestion (Alameh 2025). 77. Although I agree with the medical examiner’s finding that Ms. Moller died from complications of her unrecognized congenital heart disease—that has a recognized association with sudden cardiac death—I find that the medical examiner errs in failing to consider adequately the pharmacophysiology of the full range of substances identified on postmortem testing. 78. I find that the medical examiner errs in determining that Harmony Moller’s kratom use contributed to her death. In fact, the pharmacophysiology of kratom is more likely to be protective against cardiac sudden death in a patient such as Ms. Moller who had a high takeoff of the coronary artery with an acute angle of origin complicated by an inferior aortic flap. Following ingestion, mitragynine exerts parasympathetic effects on the cardiovascular system (Saengmolee 2022; Prevete 2024). These effects, measured generally as a slight decrease in systolic and diastolic blood pressure even in the setting of greater alertness, are insufficient to contribute to morbidity and mortality of an individual with high takeoff of the coronary artery with an acute angle of origin of the coronary artery complicated by an inferior aortic flap (Saengmolee 2022; Prevete 2024).1 79. I also find that the medical examiner errs in ignoring other substances more likely than mitragynine to worsen the congenital heart disease described in the medical record. Normally, the aorta has “elasticity,” meaning it can dilate slightly during a pulse of blood from the heart. Harmony Moller ingested caffeine. Caffeine is an over-the-counter stimulant that increases pulse rate and intra-aortic blood pressure, but caffeine also limits the elasticity (i.e., how much the blood vessel can expand in response to increased blood pressure) of the aorta. Caffeine’s pharmacologic actions make it dangerous in a person with high takeoff of the left coronary artery with an acute angle of origin. Caffeine increases aortic blood pressure and decreases aortic elasticity. These direct pharmacologic effects of caffeine compress the opening of the coronary artery precisely because the coronary artery has an acute angle of origin that narrows as the aorta expands (Virmani 1984). Moreover, the inferior aortic flap is an additional obstruction to blood flow into the coronary artery as the increased aortic blood pressure caused by caffeine presses it against the wall of the aorta. Ms. Moller’s caffeine use occluded the coronary artery and hindered blood flow into heart muscle. This decrease in cardiac perfusion caused a malignant arrhythmia culminating in sudden cardiac death. Caffeine, not mitragynine, exacerbated Ms. Moller’s congenital heart disease and contributed to her death. 80. Even if Ms. Moller was not taking her caffeine supplements, she also had “Mini Thins,” a weight-loss remedy. This product contains caffeine and yohimbine, among other plant products. Yohimbine is a presynaptic alpha-2 antagonist. The pharmacologic effects of yohimbine are to increase pulse rate and blood pressure. These direct pharmacologic effects of yohimbine, either with or without caffeine, compress the opening of the coronary artery precisely because the coronary artery has an acute angle of origin that narrows as the aorta expands (Virmani 1984). 81. Even if Harmony Moller did not die of her congenital heart disease complicated by her caffeine use, she had other, more plausible causes of death than mitragynine toxicity. For example, Ms. Moller’s vomiting was so severe that Kathleen Moller administered multiple antiemetics without improvement. Harmony Moller was taking two different caffeine-containing supplements. Caffeine is a methylxanthine. The methylxanthine toxidrome involves vomiting, seizure, and ventricular dysrthythmias (Shimane 2017). Death in methylxanthine-poisoned individuals arises from seizures or from malignant ventricular dysrhythmias (Shimane 2017; Poussel 2013). The medical examiner failed to quantify the postmortem concentration of caffeine even though Harmony Moller’s clinical presentation (i.e., severe vomiting despite multiple antiemetics before being found down with no anatomic cause of death other than her congenital heart disease) was consistent with lethal methylxanthine poisoning. This clinical presentation is also inconsistent with mitragynine toxicity. 82. Harmony Moller did not die from any contribution of mitragynine to her congenital heart disease. 83. Harmony Moller did not die from mitragynine toxicity 84. Harmony Moller did not die from her kratom use. 85. I am able to defend rigorously these conclusions, made within a reasonable degree of medical and toxicologic certainty. Dr. Williams attempts to link together all negative aspects of opioids, kratom and kratom alkaloids. He attempts unsuccessfully to establish a toxic profile of kratom alkaloids, each with an atypical corynanthe structure, by drawing parallels with formal opioids having phenanthrene, anilidopiperidine, and diphenylpropylamine chemical structures. 88. In formulating his opinions on the effects of kratom alkaloids on health, Dr. Williams picks and chooses among the scientific literature while making numerous scientific omissions and factual errors. His literature review is insufficient to allow an understanding of the complexity of kratom pharmacology, behaviors following use of the plant, or pharmacophysiologic outcomes of kratom use. 89. Dr. Williams cannot explain why kratom might contribute to Harmony Moller’s death from her congenital heart disease (that is lethal by itself), and he does not describe any putative physiologic or clinical effect of mitragynine that might directly affect Ms. Moller’s congenital heart disease. 90. Dr. Williams highlights molecules such as 7-hydroxymitragynine (a metabolite of mitragynine) and mitragynine pseudoindoxyl (a rearrangement product of 7-hydroxymitragynine). But the concentrations of neither were measured, and the medical examiner did not identify any connection between 7-hydroxymitragynine or mitragynine pseudoindoxyl and Harmony Moller’s death. Despite opining on opioid effects, Dr. Williams fails to explain how opioid activity relates to a high takeoff of the coronary artery with an acute angle of origin. 91. Dr. Williams also attempts to demonstrate that mitragynine, a metabolite (i.e., 7- hydroxymitragynine), and a rearrangement product all “rival the potency of clinically available opioids” without scientific support. Dr. Williams makes a fundamental scientific mistake by conflating ‘potency’ with ‘affinity’. 92. In his report, Dr. Williams implies that large amounts of 7-hydroxymitragynine are produced following ingestion of kratom, with a mean ratio of 0.20-0.29. This conflates parent/metabolite ratios from single dose administration and multiple dose administration. Single dose administration produces the ratio cited by Dr. Williams. Repeated ingestion of kratom by indviduals, such as Ms. Moller, produces substantially lower ratios from poorer conversion of mitragynine to 7-hydroxymitragynine (Heustis 2024). The ratio of conversion in Ms. Moller, based upon the scientific literature, is closer 0.15-.21 (Heustis 2024). Even if a higher conversion ratio occurred in Ms. Moller from intermittent use of kratom, the amount of 7-hydroxymitragynine is toxicologically irrelevant. (Chiang 2025; Hill 2021) 93. Dr. Williams states, “[T]he ingestion of Kratom yields significant amounts of both MG and 7HMG, and subsequently yields pharmacological activity associated with both compounds throughout the duration of exposure.” (Williams Report, page 3) The term “significant” carries precise scientific meanings associated with specific mathematical 13

In addition, the term “pharmacological activity” can mean anything related to the body’s handling of a xenobiotic; that these activities arise throughout the duration of exposure is unsurprising since pharmacologic activities can only occur from the moment a xenobiotic is introduced until it is totally eliminated. Finally, powdered kratom, the sort of which was used by Ms. Moller, contain small amounts of mitragyinine and a toxicologically negligible mass of 7-hydroxymitragnine (Chakraborty 2021; Zhang 2021; Smith et al., 2024). 94. While the toxicological behavior of a molecule can be explained by its pharmacology, “pharmacological activity” does not by itself equal or even connote toxicological activity. Dr. Williams cannot point to a single proven effect of kratom or any of its alkaloids that can exacerbate a high takeoff of the coronary artery with an acute angle of origin. 95. Dr. Williams claims that “cardiotoxicity has been clearly linked to . . . kratom, which includes QT prolongation,”2 citing a single case report. (Williams Report, page 4). But human studies have demonstrated daily kratom use is not associated with prolongation of the QT interval (Abdullah J. Tox 2021). Additionally, a separate human subjects study found mitragynine blood concentrations below 9,400 ng/mL were not associated with prolongation of the QT interval, and even individuals whose blood mitragynine concentration exceeded 22,000 ng/mL demonstrated slight increases in the QT interval but exhibited no cardiotoxicity. (Abdullah Frontiers in Pharmacology 2021) Unlike these studies, the single case report on which Dr. Williams relies suffers from methodologic deficiencies, including not verifying the use of kratom and relying upon standard urine drug screens to disprove use of additional substances. Moreover, the patient in Dr. Williams’s case report3 received an intervention that is different than those used to treat Torsades de Pointes, the cardiac rhythm caused by QT prolongation (Abdullah, 2019). 96. In an attempt to highlight putative effects of kratom on the QT interval, Dr. Williams cites Krantz 2023. As recognized by Dr. Williams, Krantz relies upon the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS). But there are profound shortcomings of this dataset that color the outcome of the study. These limitations include but are not limited to ambiguity about the role of the ingested xenobiotic, lack of characterization of the product, use of concomitant medications, and effect of underlying disease on outcome. Any anatomic feature that obstructs blood flow into an artery is likely to produce end organ damage. Depending on the location of the obstruction (e.g., near the takeoff of a major artery) and the organ that artery perfuses (e.g., the heart), death is a likely outcome—exactly as recognized by several publication in the medical literature (Rizzo 2021; Taylor 1992; Muriago 1997; Loukas 2016; Virmani 1984; Nishida 2014). 99. Dr. Thundiyil incorrectly states that a mitragynine blood concentration of 150 ng/mL is sufficient to be lethal. Based on the existing literature, Ms. Moller’s likely premortem concentration of mitragynine is approximately 50 ng/mL (Osawa 2025). 100. Promethazine and diphenhydramine are also known to cause QT interval prolongation when combined with other drugs or substances that can do the same. The kratom tree from Southeast Asia is related to the coffee tree, with kratom leaf powder ingested traditionally as a tea to increase energy and improve mood, like coffee. Kratom users also self-report using kratom for analgesia and to help in managing their opioid or other drug use disorder and drug withdrawal (Henningfield 2023). Kratom contains multiple alkaloids, with the primary alkaloid being mitragynine, representing approximately 2% of the plant weight (Hassan 2013). 7. Basic research, epidemiological and surveillance kratom data, and recent clinical kratom research indicate that kratom has a diverse and complex pharmacology and is not an opioid based on its chemistry, structure, or pharmacology (Kruegel 2016). 3

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 253-15 Filed 03/02/26 Page 5 of 15 8. Scientific evidence indicates that kratom should not be scheduled. After a thorough review of the evidence, the Assistant Secretary of the Department of Health and Human Services (“DHHS”), Admiral Giroir, rescinded the Food and Drug Administration (“FDA”) request to schedule kratom, mitragynine, and 7-hydroxy-mitragynine (Giroir 2018). He refuted the claims of an imminent public health risk, refuted claims of mitragynine as cause of death in FDA-cited overdoses and stated that opioid overdoses and deaths would likely increase if kratom was scheduled. 9. In a recent independent review of kratom, mitragynine, and 7-hydroxy- mitragynine, the Expert Committee on Drug Dependence, as part of the United Nations Commission on Narcotic Drugs also determined that these substances should not be scheduled due to the lack of data supporting harm (United Nations Commission on Narcotic Drugs, 2021). 10. The scientific evidence on the abuse potential of kratom, mitragynine, and 7- hydroxy-mitragynine is like many other non-scheduled compounds (Henningfield 2022a). These authors updated the 8-factor analysis for kratom, finding that there was no evidence of an imminent risk to public health, and that a Schedule I listing (the only option for substances that are not FDA- approved for therapeutic use) could produce a public health risk by increasing drug overdoses by people using kratom to abstain from opioids. We concluded that public health was better served by assuring continued access to kratom products by consumers. Kratom alkaloids and derivatives are also in development as safer and/or more effective medicines for treating pain, substance use disorders, and mood disorders. Scheduling kratom would criminalize consumers, seriously impede research, and could increase drug overdose deaths. 11. When taken responsibly, kratom offers a harm reduction tool for opioid use disorder. Dr. Nora Volkow, Director of the National Institute on Drug Abuse, testified before the U.S. Congress in May 2022 on the importance of kratom as a harm reduction tool amid the opioid overdose epidemic. In addition, individuals self-report use of kratom to help manage their opioid or other drug use disorders (NIDA 2025). Individuals who frequently consume large doses of kratom can develop kratom dependence and experience withdrawal during abstinence; however, 4

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 253-15 Filed 03/02/26 Page 6 of 15 the withdrawal is considered much milder than opioid withdrawal and is generally self-managed (Henningfield 2022a). 12. Recent preclinical data showed no respiratory depression in rats that received doses much higher than equivalent human kratom doses. Drs. Henningfield, Rodricks, Magnuson and I conducted research on the high kratom doses (up to 400 mg/kg) orally administered to rats and compared its effects to those administered oxycodone, a potent opioid (Henningfield 2022b). Oxycodone administration produced significant dose-related respiratory depressant effects and pronounced sedation with one death each at 60 and 150 mg/kg. Mitragynine did not yield significant dose-related respiratory depressant or life-threatening effects, even at the highest doses. Sedative-like effects, milder than produced by oxycodone, were evident at the 400 mg/kg dose. Consistent with mitragynine’s pharmacology that includes partial μ-opioid receptor agonism with little recruitment of the respiratory depressant activating β-arrestin pathway, mitragynine produced no evidence of respiratory depression at equivalent doses many times higher than taken by humans. 13. Recent human controlled kratom administration data established the safety and lack of abuse liability of 4000 mg oral dried kratom leaf powder doses containing up to 53.2 mg mitragynine in the first large-scale randomized, placebo-controlled, escalating single and multiple 15-day oral kratom double blind administration study in 200 healthy normal participants (Huestis 2024a). Four thousand mg dried kratom leaf powder containing 6.65 to 53.2 mg mitragynine was administered as a single dose or as 15 consecutive daily doses. As the dose of mitragynine increased, the peak concentrations of mitragynine and its metabolite, 7-hydroxy-mitragynine, increased dose-proportionally. Following a single 53.2 mg mitragynine dose in 4000 mg dried kratom leaf powder, the mean mitragynine concentration in 12 healthy normal volunteers was 130 ng/mL (range 34.2-204 ng/mL). 14. There was extensive safety monitoring of the participants throughout the 47-day study that found no serious adverse events following active single or multiple dose dried kratom leaf powder or placebo (Huestis 2024b). Treatment emergent adverse events (TEAE) were recorded if a study participant’s pre-existing condition or state changed or worsened at any time 5

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 253-15 Filed 03/02/26 Page 7 of 15 during the study regardless of whether they received a placebo or test article, therefore, TEAE may or may not be related to the study intervention. TEAE generally increased as dose increased. Steady state mitragynine and 7-hydroxy-mitragynine concentrations were achieved within seven to nine days, and drug concentrations did not accumulate greater than two-fold after multiple dosing. Dizziness, nausea and feeling of relaxation were the most common TEAE following the single kratom leaf powder dose. For context, the dietary supplement melatonin can also potentially cause dizziness, nausea, and feelings of relaxation (Mayo Clinic melatonin 2025). After multiple kratom leaf powder doses, headache, feeling hot, increased alanine transaminase concentrations and nausea were the most common TEAE (Huestis 2023). Overall, oral kratom was well-tolerated without significant cardiovascular, neurological, or hepatic adverse events. There were no seizure events in any participant across the study. The TEAE that is most closely aligned with abuse potential is euphoric mood, or an exaggerated feeling of physical and emotional well-being and optimism. Although there were sporadic, single reports of euphoric mood, there was no dose- abuse liability relationship following single kratom doses. Following the highest multiple kratom dose, there were no reports of euphoric mood, suggesting low abuse potential at the investigated doses. This study provides new safety data in humans and shows a low abuse potential at kratom doses up to 4000 mg kratom leaf powder. 15. There are few reports of kratom poisonings and overdoses in which kratom is the sole cause or a contributing cause of injuries in the United States over the past ten years based on the 2022 National Poison Data System report (Gummin 2023). In 2022, 2,064,875 human drug exposures were reported, with analgesics representing 29.6% of drug-involved exposures. Kratom/mitragynine was not classified as an analgesic in this report. Of over two million human exposures, 2,622 resulted in death that was judged to be drug-exposure related. Of these 2,622 drug exposure deaths, mitragynine was listed in only one death report (0.04%): a 25-year-old female died of a propranolol overdose with a 2000 ng/mL highly toxic propranolol blood concentration. Mitragynine was listed as contributory with a 330 ng/mL blood concentration. 6

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 253-16 Filed 03/02/26 Page 16 of 18 OVERVIEW OF MY OPINIONS Opinion 1 - People in numerous countries have used kratom (Mitragyna speciosa) safely for hundreds (if not thousands) of years. The body of scientific literature on kratom and its alkaloids continues to evolve, but historic and recent data indicate that beneficial effects associated with kratom use have a robust pharmacologic basis. It is my opinion that few to no adverse effects are expected in typical users when kratom is used alone and that adverse outcomes in dual- and polysubstance users can be attributed to other compounds, not kratom or its alkaloids. Opinion 2 - The risk assessment process is a methodology that is widely accepted and used by many scientific bodies and governmental agencies around the world. It is my opinion that it is an appropriate method to use for characterizing the health risks potentially associated with use of kratom products (especially when comparing potential health risks associated with kratom use to those associated with use of opioids to yield similar effects). Opinion 3 - The health effects of kratom can be attributed to more than 50 indole alkaloids present in the plant. Of these, mitragynine and 7-hydroxymitragynine are the most biologically significant. It is my opinion that alkaloid concentrations vary across kratom product types, but data from the peer-reviewed literature indicates that these typical concentrations contained in teas or capsules, taken in a reasonable manner, would not increase the risk of acute or chronic adverse health effects among typical users. Opinion 4 - Animal studies and studies of humans are defined as in vivo analyses. Kratom, mitragynine, 7-hydroxymitragynine, and other associated alkaloids have been studied in vivo for over 100 years. It is my opinion that these studies provide support for two primary conclusions. First, kratom and its alkaloids can yield dose-dependent stimulant or pain relief effects under typical human use and may aid with opioid withdrawal. Second, kratom alkaloids can be classified as very low to moderately toxic in animals. It is my opinion that since these alkaloids are only a small percentage of kratom products by weight, few to no adverse health effects are expected in kratom users, even among higher volume consumers. No chronic adverse 13

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 253-16 Filed 03/02/26 Page 17 of 18 effects have been reported in vivo following repeated kratom administration at relatively high doses to test animals or humans. Opinion 5 - Studies of isolated cells, termed in vitro analyses, help provide information on potential organ-specific effects and the toxicological mechanisms driving health outcomes following exposure to a given compound. In vitro data indicate that kratom alkaloids are primarily metabolized by Cytochrome P450 (CYP) isoforms CYP3A4 and CYP2D6 and that physiological effects are driven by alkaloid activity at opioid, adrenergic, serotonergic, and dopaminergic receptors. Kratom’s pain relief (analgesic) and euphoric effects can be explained by kratom alkaloid binding at opioid receptors (ORs). However, it is my opinion that the activity of mitragynine, 7-hydroxymitragynine, and other kratom alkaloids at ORs is weak relative to that of numerous drugs (e.g., morphine, fentanyl) and endogenous endorphins (e.g., β-endorphin, enkephalins, dynorphins). However, depending on the dose, 7-hydroxymitragynine can cause morphine like effects if ingested in a relatively pure state (i.e., as a synthetic isolate). Opinion 6 - Data on the effects of kratom use in humans includes epidemiological evidence, as well as information from case reports and case series. It is my opinion that human studies, although limited, indicate that kratom use is associated with potential benefits including stimulant effects, pain relief, and as a substitute or withdrawal aid for opioids at doses yielding few to no adverse behavioral or physiological effects. Case data indicate that kratom’s alkaloids produce few to no acute adverse health effects when kratom is used alone, but that mitragynine and 7-hydroxymitragynine have been reported along with other compounds in the post-mortem blood and tissues of dual- and polysubstance users. Opinion 7 - Based on the records regarding Ms. Moller’s passing, it is likely that she experienced an adverse cardiovascular event, which led to her death. Kratom has not been found to increase the risk of heart attacks in humans. It is my opinion that, should it be determined that Ms. Moller experienced a heart attack or comparable cardiovascular event which resulted in her death, kratom would not have been the cause. 14

Based on this information, it is my opinion that estimated whole- body and compartment-specific alkaloid doses for typical kratom users are 3-fold to 50,000-fold below those expected to increase the risk of adverse health effects in animals, depending on the types of products used. This is a conservative estimate, as animals are often more sensitive to potentially adverse effects of chemical exposures than humans. It is my opinion that, given the available literature, typical doses of kratom, such as the ones that Ms. Moller potentially ingested, would not increase her risk of death. Additionally, her postmortem blood concentration of mitragynine of 150 ng/mL is comparable to blood concentrations observed in human volunteers following kratom doses that are documented to be well-tolerated in humans with no adverse effects. BASES FOR OPINIONS Basis of Opinion 1 M. Speciosa Traditional Use 47. Mitragyna speciosa, commonly known as kratom, is a tree native to Southeast Asia, specifically, Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia, Borneo, Myanmar, and Vietnam. M. speciosa can reach up to 25 meters tall at maturity and is noted for having dark green leaves with green, white, or red veins (Cinosi et al. 2015). It conventionally grows in swampy areas, in areas inundated by water, and alongside riverbanks (Grundmann 2017; Ahmad et al. 2022). Depending on the country, kratom is referred to by its local name: ketum or biak (Malaysia), keton or kadamba (Indonesia), benisa (Myanmar), mambog or lugub (Philippines), ithang, thom, kratom (Thailand), or giam (Vietnam) (Gong et al. 2012; Cinosi et al. 2015; Grundmann 2017; Eastlack et al. 2020). 48. Kratom leaves were historically used in rural communities by farmers, laborers, or fishermen in Southeast Asia as a stimulant to reduce or prevent fatigue stemming from hard labor by chewing the leaves raw or drying them for later consumption (Cinosi et al. 2015; Grundmann 2017; Singh et al. 2017). On February 6, 2023, Harmony Moller was found dead at home in her room at the age of 36. See Third Amended Complaint, Dkt. No 100. 2. Discovered near her lifeless body was OPMS Green Vein Maeng Da Silver Kratom. (Exhibits 1 & 2). 3. The OPMS kratom product discovered was manufactured, imported, distributed, packaged, marketed, and sold by Defendants. (Exhibit 2).

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 253-2 Filed 03/02/26 Page 2 of 3 4. An autopsy was completed, and the death certificate lists the cause of death as abnormally high left coronary ostia takeoff exacerbated by mitragynine use. (Exhibit 15). 5. The autopsy report identifies mitragynine as a contributing factor in Harmony Moller’s death. (Exhibit 3). 6. The OPMS product label did not contain any warning that use of the product could cause death. (Exhibits 1 & 2). 7. The OPMS product label did not contain any warning regarding cardiovascular risks. Id. 8. The OPMS product label did not provide dosing instructions or maximum recommended usage amounts. Id. 9. Toxicology testing detected the presence of mitragynine in Harmony Moller’s system. (Exhibit 3). 10. Toxicology testing detected diphenhydramine and promethazine. Id. 11. The medical examiner does not identify diphenhydramine or promethazine as causes or contributing factors of death. Id. 12. No evidence in the record establishes that Harmony Moller consumed OPMS kratom in a manner inconsistent with its intended use. 13. The OPMS kratom product label did not instruct consumers to avoid using other over the counter or pharmaceutical substances when consuming its product. (Exhibits 1 & 2). Dated: March 2, 2026. Opinion 1: 22. Kratom is not and should not be characterized as “an opioid,” nor regulated as a dangerous or addictive controlled substance in the United States Controlled Substances Act (“CSA”) or under the International Drug Control Conventions of United Nations. I agree with the determinations of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (“DHHS”), DEA and the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (“UNODC”) that kratom does not warrant such designations or control. Opinion 2: 23. Kratom is not characterized by “high abuse,” “dependence” or “addiction” potential and is well within the range of many licit consumer dietary substances and health products (e.g., caffeine, antihistamines, and CBD) that are abused and can be addictive in some people but overall are used primarily for their beneficial and otherwise useful health and/or life-enhancing effects. Opinion 3: 24. Kratom does not carry a high risk of death. To the contrary, the risk of death by kratom alone appears very low and rare. This has also been the conclusion of NIDA and DEA for approximately a decade and similarly concluded by FDA in 2024 after its approximately decade of review and own testing. My opinion continues to be consistent with Assistant Secretary Gior’s 2018 review statement on this matter: “There is still debate among reputable scientists over whether kratom by itself is associated with fatal overdoses.” Opinion 4: 25. There is no consensus on the basis by which kratom might cause life threatening effects or death; in contrast to most substances that contribute to overdose deaths (e.g., respiratory depression by opioids and sedatives, cardiovascular incidents by stimulants). Opinion 5: 26. There is no consensus on what level of kratom consumption or level in the bloodstream would constitute a lethal dose, in contrast to most substances of high abuse, addiction and mortality potential that contribute to the U.S. drug overdose epidemic. Specifically, there is no well-defined toxidrome for kratom, but rather kratom associated deaths most commonly involve other substances, including prescription and non-prescribed drugs, and various pre-existing disease conditions. OPINIONS SPECIFIC TO PLAINTIFFS’ CLAIMS 35. In this section I provide opinions specific to Plaintiff’s allegations. 36. Plaintiff has not provided valid and reliable support for the allegation that kratom was the cause, or a substantial contributing factor, to Harmony Moller’s death on February 6, 2023. 37. The coroner’s report, as cited in the Complaint (para 33), suggests potential pre- existing heart abnormalities, e.g., “Abnormally high left coronary ostia takeoff.” The coroner’s report does not provide a basis for concluding that mitragynine contributed to Ms. Moller’s death. I note that blood levels of mitragynine were far lower than those that are sometimes associated with death (150 ng/mL by NMS Labs and 158 ng/mL by UC). NMS labs did not find a positive result for the mitragynine metabolite, 7-hydroxymitragynine (“7-OH”), which is consistent with low kratom/mitragynine intake. However, the NMS Labs reports did identify several other pharmacological substances and metabolites. 38. Although I do not have an opinion on the actual cause of Ms. Moller’s death, my scientific training and experience make clear that singling out kratom use as the primary or substantial contributor to death is confounded by Ms. Moller’s potential preexisting conditions and other substance use. 39. The autopsy finding that Ms. Moller’s pre-existing heart condition was “exacerbated by Mitragynine use” is speculative. There is no established scientific or medical consensus that mitragynine “exacerbates” Ms. Moller’s specific and rare cardiac anomaly or causes death in such circumstances. This is distinct from substances with well-defined mechanisms of lethal toxicity (e.g., respiratory depression from classic opioids or hypertensive crisis from classic stimulants). As Eckhardt and Nickel (2023) have concluded, “Some case reports of kratom associated arrhythmia, including fatalities, have surfaced, but little is known of the mechanism of kratom-induced ventricular arrythmia nor the depth of the problem.” 40. Attributing causation to mitragynine is confounded by (a) Ms. Moller’s pre-existing cardiac condition noted in the coroner’s report, (b) the multiple empty liquor and prescription pill bottles (including Acyclovir, methylphenidate, hydrocodone/acetaminophen, and gabapentin) and drug paraphernalia found at the scene (see St. Tammany Parish Sheriff’s Office Incident Report), 7

Huestis et al, 2024 assessed the effects of single and consecutive daily oral ascending doses of dried kratom leaf powder in healthy adults, including the mitragynine and 7- OH concentrations, over 10 days after a single dose and 23 days after multiple dosing. This was a Health Canada approved study designed to detect kratom-related adverse effects. In the trial’s highest dose group (4000mg kratom leaf powder / 53.2mg mitragynine daily for 15 days), the mean steady state peak plasma concentration (Cmax) measured was 143 ng/mL with a median of 155 ng/mL (range 64.3 – 215 ng/mL). ADDITIONAL EVIDENCE-BASED SUPPORT FOR OPINIONS Opinion 1: Kratom is not and should not be characterized as “an opioid,” nor regulated as a dangerous or addictive controlled substance in the U.S., CSA or under the International Drug Control Conventions of the United Nations. I agree with the determinations of the DEA and UNODC that kratom does not warrant such designations or control. 49. Kratom is not an opioid or narcotic by nature of its botanical origin, chemical structure or overall pharmacology and thus it is not included in the CSA or any of the United Nations International Drug Control Treaties. Nor has it ever been listed as a national drug threat in DEA’s annual National Drug Threat Assessment reports as necessary to meet statutory requirements for CSA Scheduling. Furthermore, kratom does not produce opioid-like respiratory depressant effects or the powerful euphoria that fuels the opioid epidemic. Its primary alkaloid and metabolites that do have some activity similar to opioids are partial agonists, meaning that their strongest effects are weaker than classic opioids (Henningfield et al. 2018, 2022, 2024; Kruegel et al. 2019; Kruegel et al., 2016; Henningfield and Fant, 2016; Varadi et al. 2016). 50. The DEA, NIDA, the U.S. Assistant Secretary for Health, and the WHO’s Expert Committee on Drug Dependence all agree with the conclusion that kratom is not an “opioid” and should not be scheduled as such. 51. In recent years, the FDA has been reevaluating its 2017 and 2018 statements that had suggested kratom had narcotic opioid-like effects. The FDA’s stated position as of December 2023 was that it “ha[d] not yet made a determination regarding whether kratom is dangerous.” (United States v. Nine2Five, LLC, Case No. 3:23-CR-00179-TWR (S.D. Cal.) ECF No. 110-8 at 9

Although the FDA or DEA theoretically could determine that kratom and its constituents are sufficiently pharmacologically equivalent to previously scheduled drugs such as morphine-like opioids or methamphetamine-like stimulants, the scientific evidence does not support that conclusion. INTRODUCTION Dr. Wharton’s opinions—that the decedent, Harmony Moller, died from a cardiac event induced by kratom—are inadmissible for three reasons. Plaintiff intends to present Dr. Ronald Wharton—a cardiologist with no background in toxicology, pharmacology, kratom research, or forensic pathology—to tell a jury that kratom caused Harmony Moller’s death. But under controlling Fifth Circuit precedent, an expert must be qualified in the subject matter of his opinion, must establish general causation before offering specific causation, and must apply a reliable methodology at every step. Dr. Wharton satisfies none of those requirements. 1

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 262-1 Filed 03/02/26 Page 2 of 22 First, he is not qualified to opine on kratom’s toxic effects. The Fifth Circuit requires proof of a harmful level of exposure before general causation may be presented to a jury. He failed to investigate critical medical history, failed to account for numerous other substances, failed to review key materials, and relied on assumptions rather than verified facts. The Fifth Circuit prohibits that kind of post hoc reasoning. Daubert requires intellectual rigor—not speculation, not litigation-generated hypotheses, and not conclusions reached because the expert “can’t think of anything else.” Because Dr. Wharton’s testimony fails Rule 702 at each step—qualification, general causation, and specific causation—it must be excluded in its entirety. III. ARGUMENT A. Standard for admissibility. The district court has considerable discretion to admit or exclude expert testimony under Fed. R. Evid. 702. See Gen. Elec. Co. v. Joiner, 522 U.S. 136, 138–39 (1997); Seatrax, Inc. v. Sonbeck Int’l, Inc., 200 F.3d 358, 371 (5th Cir. 2000); Tajonera v. Black Elk Energy Offshore Operations, LLC, Civ. A. No. 13-0366, 2016 WL 3180776, at *8 (E.D. La. June 7, 2016) (Brown, J.) (citing authority). The burden rests with the party seeking to present the testimony to show that the requirements of Rule 702 are met. Moore v. Ashland Chemical, Inc., 151 F.3d 269, 276 (5th Cir. 1998). Rule 702 provides that an expert witness “qualified . . . by knowledge, skill, experience, training, or education may testify in the form of an opinion” when the following requirements are met: 9

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 262-1 Filed 03/02/26 Page 10 of 22 (a) The expert’s scientific, technical, or other specialized knowledge will help the trier of fact to understand the evidence or to determine a fact in issue; (b) The testimony is based on sufficient facts or data; (c) The testimony is the product of reliable principles and methods; and (d) The expert has reliably applied the principles and methods to the facts of the case. Fed. R. Evid. 702. Rule 702 codifies the Supreme Court’s opinion in Daubert, which charges district courts to act as “gatekeeper” when determining the admissibility of expert testimony. Tajonera, 2016 WL 3180776, at *8. The purpose of a Daubert motion is “to ensure that only reliable and relevant expert testimony is presented to the jury.” Rushing v. Kansas City S. Ry. Co., 185 F.3d 496, 506 (5th Cir. 1999) (superseded by rule on other grounds) (citing Daubert, 509 U.S. at 590–93). When an injury was allegedly caused by a substance, the Fifth Circuit applies a two-step framework to examine the admissibility of causation evidence. Knight v. Kirby Inland Marine, Inc., 482 F.3d 347, 351 (5th Cir. 2007). First, the court must determine whether there is admissible evidence of general causation: that “a substance is capable of causing a particular injury.” Id. Second, if the court “concludes that there is admissible general-causation evidence, [it] must determine whether there is admissible specific-causation evidence.” Id. Critically, “[e]vidence concerning specific causation . . . is admissible only as a follow-up to admissible general-causation evidence.” Id. The Court’s inquiry is whether the expert’s reasoning is reliable at each step. Knight, 482 F.3d at 355. Opinions based on assumptions, speculation, or gaps between the data and the conclusion are inadmissible. Id.; Viterbo v. Dow Chem. Co., 826 F.2d 420, 424 (5th Cir. 1987). 10

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 262-1 Filed 03/02/26 Page 11 of 22 The proponent must prove admissibility by a preponderance, and “expert’s assurances” do not substitute for objective reliability. Moore, 151 F.3d at 276. B. Dr. Wharton is not qualified to offer his causation opinions in this case. Dr. Wharton is a cardiologist. He is not trained in toxicology, pharmacology, forensic pathology, or kratom research. Yet, he proposes to tell a jury that kratom’s active compounds caused a death. That opinion is outside his expertise, outside his training, and outside the limits Rule 702 imposes on expert testimony. Rule 702 does not allow a witness to leverage general medical credentials into authority over an entirely different scientific field. An expert “may not go beyond the scope of his expertise in giving his opinion.” MGMTL, LLC v. Strategic Tech. Inst., Inc., 2022 WL 485279, at *6 (E.D. La. Feb. 17, 2022) (Vitter, CJ). Dr. Wharton does precisely that by offering opinions on the specific chemical properties of mitragynine and its effect on the human body—a subject he knew nothing about before this litigation, and still does not, as demonstrated in his deposition. His lack of expertise in the relevant fields is the first of many reasons his testimony should be excluded. See Moore, 151 F.3d at 276. In Moore, the Fifth Circuit affirmed the exclusion of an expert based on the district court’s conclusion that the bases for their opinion was “individually and collectively inadequate” under Daubert. Id. at 277. The excluded expert’s “training and experience . . . were obviously important to his diagnosis” but he “gave no reason why these items were helpful in reaching his conclusion on causation” and “admitted that he had never previously treated a patient who had been exposed to a similar Toluene solution” – the solution that was alleged to cause the harm. Id. at 277–78. The Court noted the excluded expert “was a highly qualified pulmonary specialist, but, as the Seventh Circuit observed in Rosen v. This is precisely the kind of expert overreach Daubert is designed to prevent. A cardiologist may testify about cardiac structure and disease. He may not step into the role of toxicologist simply because the case involves a heart. Dr. Wharton admitted he had never studied kratom, never treated a kratom exposure, never researched its pharmacology, and learned about it only after being retained for this case. Allowing him to testify anyway would present the jury with the imprimatur of medical authority untethered to actual expertise. Rule 702 requires more than credentials—it requires qualification in the subject at issue. Because Dr. Wharton lacks that qualification, his kratom causation opinions must be excluded. C. Dr. Wharton failed to establish general causation before opining on specific causation. Even assuming Dr. Wharton is qualified to address cardiac physiology, his general- causation opinions are independently inadmissible under Rule 702. Fifth Circuit precedent requires reliable scientific evidence identifying a harmful level of exposure before causation testimony may be presented to a jury. Dr. Wharton concedes that no such dose is known here. That failure is dispositive. The Fifth Circuit requires admissible general-causation evidence before any specific- causation testimony may be admitted. Johnson v. Arkema, Inc., 685 F.3d 453, 469 (5th Cir. 2012); Knight, 482 F.3d at 351. At a minimum, general causation requires scientific knowledge of a harmful level of exposure. Johnson, 685 F.3d at 469; Allen, 102 F.3d at 199. Dr. Wharton must therefore identify “the harmful level of exposure” to mitragynine that is capable of causing a fatal arrhythmia in the general population. Kaoui v. BP Expl. & Prod., Inc., No. CV 17-3313, 2023 WL 13

He admitted he does not know what constitutes either a safe or lethal dose. Ex. 2, Wharton Dep. at 71:22–72:25. Dr. Wharton acknowledged that his opinion is “based on reasonable speculation” and “his experience as a cardiologist” as “[w]e have no hard data on a drug or agent of this nature.” Id. at 167:10–170:21. Dr. Wharton claims that scientific literature suggests a “linkage between the main alkaloid in Mitragyna speciosa (kratom) use, ventricular arrhythmias (ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation) and cardiorespiratory adverse events” and “potentially fatal effects on the electrocardiogram attributed to the use of kratom.” Ex. 1, Initial Report, 2–3. This opinion fails to establish general causation for several reasons. First, as noted above, the one article he cites for his opinion concludes “a lack of a convincing mechanistic link between mitragynine and ventricular arrhythmia” and state “causal determinations cannot be made.” Ex. 2, Wharton Dep. at 191:7-194:12. Thus, the study does not identify the harmful level at which physical symptoms manifest though that was an object of the study. Thus, Dr. Wharton fails to cite evidence of general causation. Kaoui, 2023 WL 330510, at *6 (“To establish general causation, a causation expert must identify ‘the harmful level of exposure to a chemical’ at which physical symptoms manifest.”). This Court has stressed, “nearly every chemical on Earth may be toxic or even fatal at a certain level of exposure,” so “[c]ausation experts determine not only whether a chemical is capable of causing certain health effects, but at what level of exposure do those health affects appear.” Id. “[F]ailure to properly identify the level of exposure to a particular chemical at which harmful effects occur necessarily renders a general causation opinion to be unreliable and, thus, inadmissible.” Id. 14

The MSDS made it clear that the effects of exposure to Toluene depended on the concentration and length of exposure.”). Where assumptions substitute for facts—such as, for example, exposure, as here—causation devolves into “mere guesswork” and is inadmissible. Seaman v. Seacor Marine L.L.C., 326 F. App’x 721, 727–28 (5th Cir. 2009) (affirming exclusion where assumptions about exposure levels rendered causation opinion “mere guesswork” and failed to establish either general or specific causation). Even assuming Dr. Wharton is qualified in his own field, his general-causation opinions must be excluded because they fail the Fifth Circuit’s most basic reliability requirement: identifying a scientifically established harmful level of exposure. D. Dr. Wharton's specific causation opinion is unreliable. Even if Dr. Wharton could establish general causation—which he cannot—his specific causation opinion independently fails under Rule 702 because it rests on a fundamentally unreliable “process of elimination.” He admitted that he concluded kratom caused Harmony Moller’s death because he “can’t think of anything else that would have done this.” Ex. 2, Wharton Dep. at 218:10–14. That is not science. It is guesswork. 1. The Fifth Circuit has rejected this exact methodology. An expert may eliminate alternative causes only after establishing that the substance at issue is capable of causing the injury and only if the elimination itself is performed in a scientifically reliable manner. Where either step fails, the opinion is inadmissible. 15

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 262-1 Filed 03/02/26 Page 16 of 22 Dr. Wharton characterizes his method as a “differential diagnosis,” which he agrees requires systematically eliminating “any other possible cause.” Ex. 2, Wharton Dep. at 248:14– 249:24. But the Fifth Circuit has made clear that process-of-elimination reasoning is not admissible unless it is anchored in reliable scientific groundwork. In Black v. Food Lion, Inc., the Fifth Circuit excluded expert testimony where the expert concluded that because she had ruled out other possible causes, the remaining event “had to be” the cause. 171 F.3d 308, 313 (5th Cir. 1999). Id. The Court explained, “This analysis amounts to saying that because [the expert] thought she had eliminated other possible causes of [the condition], even though she does not know the real ‘cause,’ it had to be the [injury-causing event]. This is not an exercise in scientific logic but in the fallacy of post-hoc propter-hoc reasoning.” The Fifth Circuit further held that such a “general methodology cannot vindicate a conclusion for which there is no underlying medical support.” Id. at 314. That is precisely what happened here. Dr. Wharton does not identify a scientifically established harmful dose of mitragynine. He does not establish a validated mechanism of death tied to a known exposure level. Instead, he assumes kratom must be responsible because he does not see a better explanation. That is the same reasoning rejected in Black. A differential diagnosis is not a free pass. It is admissible only when the expert reliably establishes general causation and then methodically rules out alternatives based on complete and accurate data. It is not admissible when it functions as a fallback after scientific proof fails. 2. Dr. Wharton did not reliably rule out obvious alternative causes. Even if process-of-elimination reasoning were theoretically permissible here, Dr. Wharton did not perform it reliably. He acknowledged that both promethazine and diphenhydramine were present in Harmony Moller’s system—drugs known to prolong the QT interval—yet he offers no 16

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 262-1 Filed 03/02/26 Page 17 of 22 scientifically grounded basis for concluding kratom was the decisive agent. He admitted he had not reviewed critical materials, including crime scene photographs showing numerous substances present at the scene. Those substances included vaping devices, alcohol, prescription medications, supplements, caffeine products, marijuana products, and unidentified materials. He testified that he “would want to know what the substance is because that’s the only way you could determine what its potential for adverse effects are,” yet he did not know what many of those substances were. That alone defeats any claim of systematic elimination. He further admitted he “forgot the THC” in his report. When asked about ondansetron— another drug potentially associated with QT prolongation—he stated that “[i]f it does, we can add it.” Wharton Dep. at 130:10–132:16. That is not a defined methodology. That is improvisation. His approach effectively operates as a one-way ratchet: any substance known to prolong QT can be added to support causation, but none is rigorously evaluated as an independent cause. Meanwhile, kratom is treated as sufficient without a scientifically established dose-response foundation. 3. Dr. Wharton failed to investigate critical medical and physiologic factors. Dr. Wharton also relied on assumptions that collapse under scrutiny. He asserted that there was no relevant family history of premature sudden cardiac death, yet he was unaware that Ms. Moller’s brother died unexpectedly in his 30s and does not know the cause. For a cardiologist opining on arrhythmia, failure to investigate family cardiac history is not a minor omission—it is a fundamental methodological flaw. He also assumed Harmony Moller had “no recent medical illnesses and no chronic medical conditions,” yet admitted he did not know her physical condition in the days and hours before her death. Records reflect reports of vomiting and possible food poisoning—conditions known to 17

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 262-1 Filed 03/02/26 Page 18 of 22 cause electrolyte imbalance and trigger ventricular arrhythmias. He acknowledged that such electrolyte disturbances can precipitate arrhythmias. Yet he did not analyze or rule out this pathway. That is not systematic exclusion. It is selective omission. 4. Dr. Wharton’s approach is guesswork disguised as expertise. Rule 702 requires intellectual rigor. Kumho Tire Co. v. Carmichael, 526 U.S. 137, 152 (1999). It requires the court to ensure reliability at every step. Knight, 482 F.3d at 355. Dr. Wharton did not establish a harmful kratom exposure threshold, did not reliably quantify competing substances, did not investigate known arrhythmia triggers, did not review critical medical history, was not aware of Harmony’s physical condition prior to death, and relied on assumptions about toxicology screening. When elimination rests on incomplete information and untested assumptions, it is not differential diagnosis—it is “mere guesswork.” Seaman, 326 F. App’x at 727–28. The Fifth Circuit has already warned against exactly this maneuver: using temporal sequence and absence of a preferred alternative as proof of causation. Black, 171 F.3d at 313–15. That is what Dr. Wharton has done here. His specific causation opinion should be excluded. 5. Dr. Wharton’s approach fails Daubert. Even apart from the Fifth Circuit’s squarely on-point holding in Black, Dr. Wharton’s methodology collapses under the core Daubert reliability factors. What remains is not scientific reasoning but subjective belief dressed as expert testimony. Moore, 151 F.3d at 277–79 (affirming exclusion where “[n]one of Daubert’s factors to assess whether the opinion was based on sound scientific principles was met”). In Moore, the expert could cite “no scientific support” for the proposition that exposure to irritants at unknown levels caused the alleged harm. The Fifth Circuit 18

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 262-1 Filed 03/02/26 Page 19 of 22 held that such speculation “lacking any scientific validity” must be excluded. Id. That principle applies with equal force here. First, Dr. Wharton’s core theory—that a post-mortem mitragynine concentration of 150 ng/mL alone caused Ms. Moller’s death while superseding her documented coronary anomaly and the presence of other substances—is a litigation-generated hypothesis. It has never been tested. It cannot be tested. There is no established exposure threshold, no validated dose-response curve, and no empirical method by which his conclusion could be verified or falsified. Second, his dismissal of Ms. Moller’s “abnormally high left coronary ostia takeoff” as a “benign finding,” (Ex. 1, Initial Report, at 3), despite the coroner’s contrary conclusion, is not grounded in peer-reviewed authority. He has identified no literature validating that conclusion under these circumstances. When pressed in deposition, he conceded that it was not his “job” to provide supporting references. That is not expert methodology. It is assertion. Daubert requires more than credentials and confidence. Third, there is no identifiable protocol for testing Dr. Wharton’s case-specific, multi- variable theory. Without a defined methodology, there is no measurable rate of error. There are no governing standards. There is no control against confirmation bias. Those are classic markers of courtroom-driven speculation, not reliable science. Fourth, even accepting differential diagnosis as a generally accepted clinical tool, Dr. Wharton did not apply it reliably. A proper differential diagnosis requires systematic consideration and exclusion of all plausible causes. He failed to do that. He did not fully evaluate the independent arrhythmogenic potential of other QT-prolonging drugs present. He admitted he “forgot” certain substances and was willing to “add” others after the fact. He did not meaningfully assess the decedent’s vomiting and possible dehydration—well-known triggers of electrolyte 19

His process was not structured elimination; it was selective omission. Finally, even if differential diagnosis is generally accepted in medicine, this version of it is not. The relevant medical community would not accept a causation opinion that: (1) lacks a known harmful dose, (2) ignores competing pharmacologic effects, (3) fails to evaluate documented physiologic stressors, and (4) dismisses structural cardiac findings without supporting literature. General acceptance does not attach to an expert’s flawed application of a method. It attaches only to a reliable execution of it. Dr. Wharton has offered a conclusion in search of support. He admitted he does not know what a safe or lethal dose of mitragynine is. Ex. 2, Wharton Dep. at 71:22–72:25. Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 262-2 Filed 03/02/26 Page 3 of 12 Specifically, you requested my opinion as to the cause of the sudden death of Harmony Moller. It is my opinion that Harmony Moller, an otherwise healthy 36-year-old young woman, suffered a cardiorespiratory cause of death on February 6, 2023. Pertinent Medical History: It is my understanding that the decedent was found on autopsy to have what was described as “abnormally high left coronary ostia takeoff exacerbated by mitragynine use”. It is also my understanding that Harmony Moller had no prodrome prior to her being found pulseless by her mother in the early morning hours. She had no recent medical illness and no chronic medical conditions, as was confirmed at autopsy. I have also been asked to assume that Harmony Moller had resided in Southeast Asia as a teacher for some thirteen years, returning to the United States in 2021 to help care for her ailing father prior to his death. Apparently, while there, Harmony Moller had consumed natural Mitragyna speciosa leaf and, upon returning, purchased and consumed kratom sold in local stores in the area where she lived in Louisiana. The toxicology report confirmed the presence of mitragynine (150 ng/mL) in her femoral blood. Discussion: There are multiple reports in the medical literature that associate the use of kratom products with the development of ventricular tachycardia and ventricular fibrillation (VT/VF), which cause the heart to stop beating. This leads to the immediate cessation of circulation and death within a few minutes unless treated with defibrillation. My opinion is based on exclusion, as a cardiorespiratory death, such as cardiac arrhythmia, cannot be confirmed by autopsy or postmortem toxicology. Sudden death occurs from either an anatomic or a toxic/metabolic cause. No anatomic cause (traumatic, cardiac, thromboembolic, or neurologic) was identified. There is no medical history of any condition that would cause a dangerous metabolic derangement (there were no chronic medical conditions identified at autopsy), nor was there any family history of premature sudden cardiac death. Cardiac adverse events such as VT/VF can be precipitated by exogenous substances. A comprehensive review of opioid-associated arrhythmia in North America published in the Journal of the American College of Cardiology in 2023 by Krantz et. al.1 demonstrated a “disproportionate” association of “life threatening arrhythmias in North America” with mitragynine. While data and research into kratom is evolving, the literature discussing kratom consumption and its effects suggests a significant linkage between the main alkaloid in 2

In March 2025, potentially fatal effects on the electrocardiogram attributed to the use of kratom were published3,4. Conclusions: 1. Harmony Moller had no known signs or symptoms of chronic or acute disease or injury presaging her sudden death prior to her demise on February 6, 2023. 2. The high ostia take-off of the left coronary artery is a benign finding which was not a cause of her sudden death. 3. In my opinion, more likely than not, Harmony Moller died from a cardiorespiratory adverse event induced by consumption of kratom. Causeway Approach Mandeville, LA 70471 RE: Katherine Moller o/b/o Harmony Moller (D) v Martian Sales, Inc., et al; US District Court, Eastern District of Louisiana; Civil Action NO. 24-0228-WBV-DPC Dear Mr. Wagar: This is a follow-up to my initial report dated October 19, 2025. You have asked that I opine on the reports of Drs. Allen L. Dollar, Dr. Amber Wang, and Dr. Winston Gandy Jr. Since the opinions of these physicians are based upon toxicology and the post-mortem macroscopic and microscopic findings at autopsy, I would first like to summarize what I believe to be the pertinent findings: 1) It is known that Ms. Moller had a “high takeoff” of the left coronary artery. 2) Promethazine was found at a concentration of 18 ng/cc. 3) Diphenhydramine was found at a concentration of 64 ng/cc 4) Microscopic pathology noted “section of ventricular septum has normal arrangement of myocytes within the compact myocardium. Myocytes are hypertrophic and there are scattered hypereosinophilic myocytes.” There were findings noted in the macroscopic pathology which I will address below. My responses are as follows: 1) The “high takeoff of the left coronary artery” is not associated with sudden cardiac death (as an aside, the pathology report makes no mention of an “interarterial or intramural course” of the left coronary artery). The known anomaly associated with sudden death is that in which the left coronary artery takes its origin from the right coronary cusp and in doing so courses between the aorta and the main pulmonary artery, which is not the case here. Furthermore, those coronary anomalies which are associated with sudden death do so during periods of exertion. 2) Promethazine and diphenhydramine can prolong the QT-interval. There is a growing body of evidence that molecules present in Kratom prolong the QT-interval. 3) The hallmark of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is the presence of myocardial disarray. A “normal arrangement of myocytes” is not compatible with the presence of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, nor is the presence of “eosinophilic myocytes”. It is standard of care to caution patients about polypharmacy which could have adverse synergistic effects. This is certainly true when considering the potential for QT

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 262-6 Filed 03/02/26 Page 3 of 4 prolongation. Even if the concentration of an individual agent is considered not to be dangerous, when multiple agents are taken together, there is a risk for dangerous QT prolongation which can result in polymorphic ventricular tachycardia. The pathology report is not consistent with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM). a) The left ventricle was reported as “mildly dilated”. The left ventricular cavity in patients with HCM is small, and certainly not “dilated”. b) The heart’s weight was reported as only 10 grams above the reference range. c) There is a growing body of evidence linking Kratom use to hypertension, which could lead to hypertensive heart disease (i.e. left ventricular hypertrophy)1. It is certainly possible that the left ventricular hypertrophy noted at autopsy was a manifestation of Kratom exposure. d) Myocardial disarray, the hallmark of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, was not found in the microscopic pathology. This finding is associated with dangerous arrhythmias2,3. The absence of this finding precludes the diagnosis of HCM. e) Those risk factors for sudden death in patients with a history of HCM about which we have knowledge (left ventricular wall thickness > 30 mm, family history of sudden cardiac death, left ventricular apical aneurysm, unexplained syncope) are decidedly absent. The combination of promethazine, diphenhydramine, and Kratom can synergistically lead to QT interval prolongation and consequent polymorphic ventricular tachycardia. Conclusions: 1. The high ostia take-off of the left coronary artery is a benign finding which was not a cause of her sudden death. 2. The pathology report, both macroscopic and microscopic, is inconsistent with a diagnosis of HCM. 3. In my opinion, more likely than not, Harmony Moller died from a ventricular arrhythmia induced by consumption of Kratom, especially in combination with two other agents known to prolong the QT interval. The conclusions reached in this report are based on my education, training, and experience, and are all within reasonable medical probability. This report is based on the material I have been asked to review as of January 2, 2026. I am being compensated at a rate of $700/hr for my consultation in this case. I reserve the right to amend this report should further information become available. Ronald H. Ventricular Arrhythmias Associated With Over-the-Counter and Recreational Opioids Mori J. Krantz, MD,a,b Todd J. Rudo, MD,a Mark C.P. Haigney, MD,c Norman Stockbridge, MD, PHD,d Robert B. Kleiman, MD,a Michael Klein, PHD,c David P. Kao, MDe ABSTRACT BACKGROUND Epidemic increases in opioid deaths prompted policies limiting access to prescription opioids in North America. Consequently, the over-the-counter opioids loperamide (Imodium A-D) and mitragynine, the herbal ingredient in kratom, are increasingly used to avert withdrawal or induce euphoria. Arrhythmia events related to these nonscheduled drugs have not been systematically studied. OBJECTIVES In this study, we sought to explore opioid-associated arrhythmia reporting in North America. METHODS The U.S. Food and Drug Administration Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS), Center for Food Safety and Applied Nutrition Adverse Event Reporting System (CAERS), and Canada Vigilance Adverse Reaction (CVAR) data- bases were searched (2015-2021). Reports involving nonprescription drugs (loperamide, mitragynine) and diphenoxylate/ atropine (Lomotil) were identiﬁed. Methadone, a prescription opioid (full agonist), served as a positive control owing to its established arrhythmia risk. Buprenorphine (partial agonist) and naltrexone (pure antagonist), served as negative controls. Reports were classiﬁed according to Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities terminology. Signiﬁcant disproportionate reporting required a proportional reporting ratio (PRR) of $2, $3 cases, and chi-square $4. Primary analysis used FAERS data, whereas CAERS and CVAR data were conﬁrmatory. RESULTS Methadone was disproportionately associated with ventricular arrhythmia reports (PRR: 6.6; 95% CI: 6.2-7.0; n ¼ 1,163; chi-square ¼ 5,456), including 852 (73%) fatalities. Loperamide was also signiﬁcantly associated with arrhythmia (PRR: 3.2; 95% CI: 3.0-3.4; n ¼ 1,008; chi-square ¼ 1,537), including 371 (37%) deaths. Mitragynine demonstrated the highest signal (PRR: 8.9; 95% CI: 6.7-11.7; n ¼ 46; chi-square ¼ 315), with 42 (91%) deaths. Bupre- norphine, diphenoxylate, and naltrexone were not associated with arrhythmia. Signals were similar in CVAR and CAERS. CONCLUSIONS The nonprescription drugs loperamide and mitragynine are associated with disproportionate reports of life-threatening ventricular arrhythmia in North America. DEFENDANTS’ MEMORANDUM SUPPORT OF MOTION TO EXCLUDE PLAINTIFF’S EXPERT JOSEF G. THUNDIYIL UNDER FED. RULE OF EVID. 702 Defendant JOpen, LLC (“Defendant” or “JOpen”) hereby files this Motion to Exclude Plaintiff’s Expert Witness, Dr. Josef G. Thundiyil, under Federal Rule of Evidence 702 and Daubert v. Merrell Dow Pharmaceuticals, Inc., 509 U.S. 579 (1993) and incorporated memorandum of law. I. INTRODUCTION Plaintiff has designated Dr. Thundiyil to offer causation opinions that: (1) “Harmony Moller’s cause of death was an adverse cardiorespiratory event caused by kratom” and (2) “Harmony Moller did not cause her own death.” Ex. 1, Nov. 18, 2025 Expert Report of Dr. Josef Thundiyil, at 8, 11. This is a toxic-tort case. Under controlling Fifth Circuit law, Plaintiff cannot present a causation expert to the jury unless that expert first establishes reliable general causation—that kratom is capable of causing the type of fatal event alleged here at the levels present in this case. Only then may the expert attempt to prove specific causation. Dr. Thundiyil cannot clear that first gate. He concedes that “we don’t know the exact level 1

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 265-1 Filed 03/02/26 Page 2 of 17 [of kratom] that causes toxicity,” and that it is “nearly impossible … with the existing science, to have a dose that we know causes harm.” Ex. 2, Excerpts from Thundiyil Dep. 146:8–9, 147:3–5, Jan. 16, 2026. He admits he cannot identify a fatal dose range, cannot reliably extrapolate from post-mortem levels to antemortem exposure, and cannot determine whether the death sequence was cardiac-first or respiratory-first. Those admissions are not minor weaknesses. They eliminate the foundational element required by the Fifth Circuit. Despite these concessions, Dr. Thundiyil proposes to tell the jury that the mitragynine concentration in this case was “sufficient to cause adverse events” and that kratom caused Harmony Moller’s death. Ex. 1, at 10. That is the precise analytical leap the Fifth Circuit forbids: an inference that bridges an admitted dose-response void with nothing more than conclusion. The methodological defect deepens at the specific-causation step. Dr. Thundiyil purports to conduct a differential diagnosis, but he applies a quantitative standard to exclude alternative causes while admitting no such scientifically established threshold exists for kratom. He rejects THC, diphenhydramine, and promethazine because they were not present at a “fatal or toxic” level, yet cannot identify any fatal or toxic level for kratom itself. Id. That is not differential diagnosis; it is a one-directional inference that treats kratom as sufficient without reliable science while dismissing alternatives under a standard he cannot consistently apply. His invocation of “Bradford Hill” does not cure these defects. He admits the analysis was only performed “mentally,” without a step-by-step application, documentation, or testable framework. Rule 702 does not permit experts to substitute an unarticulated mental checklist for reproducible methodology. Courts evaluate what an expert actually did, not what he calls it. Under Rule 702 and binding Fifth Circuit precedent, this Court must ensure reliability “at each and every step.” Knight v. Kirby Inland Marine, Inc., 482 F.3d 347, 355 (5th Cir. 2007). 2

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 265-1 Filed 03/02/26 Page 3 of 17 Because Dr. Thundiyil cannot establish general causation, cannot reliably apply specific causation, and cannot consistently rule out alternatives under a defensible scientific framework, his causation opinions are inadmissible and must be excluded in full. II. FACTUAL BACKGROUND This is a products liability case in which Plaintiff alleges that O.P.M.S. Silver kratom caused Harmony Moller’s death on February 6, 2023. See ECF. No. 100, at ¶¶ 30, 33. Specifically, Plaintiff claims that Defendants designed an inherently and unreasonably dangerous product, that Defendants failed to adequately warn of the dangers associated with O.P.M.S. Silver kratom, and that Defendants failed to provide adequate instructions on how to avoid such risks. See ECF No. 100, at ¶ 61. It is undisputed that the level of mitragynine in Harmony’s blood after death was very low: 150 ng/mL. Ex. 1, at 10. Dr. Thundiyil is a licensed medical doctor practicing in the state of Florida, with Board Certifications in Emergency Medicine, Medical Toxicology, and Occupation and Environmental Medicine. Ex. 1, at 1. He presents himself “as an expert in both acute management of medical conditions (Emergency Medicine) and the effects of chemicals and substances on the human health (Medical Toxicology).” Id. Dr. Thundiyil was retained by Plaintiff to provide expert opinions on Harmony Moller’s “death and the cause of her death, including the impact of and causative nature of Defendants’ [] kratom products.” Id. During Dr. Thundiyil’s deposition, counsel for Defendant’s “asked the doctor whether he had ever performed any studies related to kratom, and he described an unpublished study from 2020 to 2024 looking at reported deaths in Florida from kratom as compared to a control group of patients that died in Orange County, Florida, who had kratom or mitragynine on board, but whose causes of death were not attributed to those substances.” ECF No. 236, Order and Reasons, at 2. 3

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 265-1 Filed 03/02/26 Page 4 of 17 The Court found that Plaintiff “failed” to comply with her obligations under Rule 26(a)(2)(B) to disclose “a complete and accurate written report by Dr. Thundiyil” and that “[g]ood cause” exists to allow a second deposition of Dr. Thundiyil and the disclosure and production of facts or data related to his study. ECF No. 236, at 14–15. The Court set a production deadline of March 3, 2026 and a deadline for completion of the second deposition of Dr. Thundiyil of March 6, 2026. Id. Accordingly, Defendants reserve the right to supplement the arguments herein based on the findings from this additional study. This includes challenging Dr. Thundiyil’s qualifications as an expert on the pharmacology of kratom or risk profile of Kratom. In his report, Dr. Thundiyil concludes that the circumstances of Harmony Moller’s death “support[] the conclusion that Harmony Moller died from an adverse cardiorespiratory event caused by kratom.” Ex. 1, at 10. He asserts “[t]he toxicology results from NMS Labs directly support kratom’s causative role” in the death and that the post-mortem blood concentration of mitragynine was “a level sufficient to cause adverse events.” Id. He also offers the following opinions regarding other substances: (i) that “[t]he toxicology results also returned a positive result for caffeine, a finding expected in individual who ingested caffeinated products such as coffee; (ii) Delta-9 THC and Delta-9 Carboxy THC were “present at low levels” that are “not consistent with a toxic or fatal ingestion”; (iii) diphenhydramine (present at a concentration of 64 ng/ml) and promethazine (present at a concentration of 18 ng/ml) are “not consistent with a fatal or toxic dose” and “consistent with therapeutic dosing,” and thus, “unlikely to be a cause or contributor of Harmony Moller’s death.” Id. Joiner, 522 U.S. 136, 138–39 (1997); Seatrax, Inc. v. Sonbeck Int’l, Inc., 200 F.3d 358, 371 (5th Cir. 2000); Tajonera v. Black Elk Energy Offshore Operations, LLC, Civ. A. No. 13-0366, 2016 WL 3180776, at *8 (E.D. La. June 7, 2016) (Brown, J.) (citing authority). The burden rests with the party seeking to present the testimony to show that 5

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 265-1 Filed 03/02/26 Page 6 of 17 the requirements of Rule 702 are met. Moore v. Ashland Chemical, Inc., 151 F.3d 269, 276 (5th Cir. 1998). Rule 702 provides that an expert witness “qualified . . . by knowledge, skill, experience, training, or education may testify in the form of an opinion” when the following requirements are met: (a) The expert’s scientific, technical, or other specialized knowledge will help the trier of fact to understand the evidence or to determine a fact in issue; (b) The testimony is based on sufficient facts or data; (c) The testimony is the product of reliable principles and methods; and (d) The expert has reliably applied the principles and methods to the facts of the case. Fed. R. Evid. 702. Rule 702 codifies the Supreme Court’s opinion in Daubert, which charges district courts to act as “gatekeeper” when determining the admissibility of expert testimony. Tajonera, 2016 WL 3180776, at *8. The purpose of a Daubert motion is “to ensure that only reliable and relevant expert testimony is presented to the jury.” Rushing v. Kansas City S. Ry. Co., 185 F.3d 496, 506 (5th Cir. 1999) (superseded by rule on other grounds) (citing Daubert, 509 U.S. at 590–93). In the Fifth Circuit, Thundiyil’s opinions are inadmissible because they lack a reliable foundation.1 The Fifth Circuit requires a two-step showing: general causation first (that a 1 “Plaintiff bears the obligation to disclose a complete and accurate written report by Dr. Thundiyil as described under Rule 26(a)(2)(B).” ECF No. 236, Order and Reasons, at 14–15. Where assumptions substitute for facts—such as, for example, exposure, as here—causation devolves into “mere guesswork” and is inadmissible. Seaman v. Seacor Marine L.L.C., 326 F. App’x 721, 727– 28 (5th Cir. 2009) (affirming exclusion where assumptions about exposure levels rendered causation opinion “mere guesswork” and failed to establish either general or specific causation). Even apart from his foundational failure on general causation, Dr. Thundiyil’s specific- causation opinion rests on inputs that cannot be determined. He acknowledged that redistribution of kratom in the deceased’s body following death can cause mitragynine levels to appear higher or lower than they were before death—“it can actually go both ways.” Ex. 2, at 209:11–22. These are not minor uncertainties. They go to the core of the causation analysis. The Fifth Circuit repeatedly warns that courts must exclude medical testimony where the expert cannot reliably connect the scientific literature to the facts of the case. Knight, 482 F.3d at 355. That is precisely the “analytical gap” Daubert forbids. Black is particularly instructive. There, the Fifth Circuit rejected the precise type of testimony Thundiyil wants to give here—the inference that because symptoms (or an injury) followed an exposure, the exposure must have caused the injury. Black, at 171 F.3d at 313. In Black, the plaintiff slipped on mayonnaise at a grocery store and claimed the fall caused 13

OPINIONS AND BASIS THEREOF These opinions are given to a reasonable degree of medical certainty. a. Harmony Moller’s cause of death was an adverse cardiorespiratory event caused by kratom. Kratom is the common term for Mitragyna speciosa, a tree that is native to Southeast Asia. In traditional preparations, kratom leaves are used in tea as an herbal medicine for various medical conditions including pain and increased energy. In the United States, the commercially sold kratom often takes the form of processed powders and extracts. Both the effect and toxicity of kratom are dose related.
